passages.t: Before the battle: who may go home
passages.happening:
Moses gives rules for war. First, a word against fear. When Israel sees ‘horses, chariots, and an army larger than yours’, it is not to be afraid, ‘for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you’ (verse 1).

Before battle the priest is to speak to the army. “Hear, O Israel, today you are going into battle with your enemies. Do not be fainthearted or afraid” (verse 3). “For the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory” (verse 4).

Then the officers ask four questions. Has any man built a new house and not yet lived in it? Planted a vineyard and not yet tasted its fruit? Promised to marry a woman and not yet married her? Each is told, ‘Let him return home’ (verses 5-7). And last: “Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home, so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Israel had no standing army at this time. Its soldiers were farmers and tradesmen called up from their villages. That is why these rules matter.

The priest's speech begins with the first words of the Shema, ‘Hear, O Israel’. Before a battle Israel is called to remember who its God is. Horses and chariots were the heavy weapons of the day. The army is told that its strength lies elsewhere.

Then the surprising part. The officers go through the ranks sending men home. A house, a vineyard and a marriage are the ordinary goods of life in the land. A new vineyard took several years to bear. The law will not let war rob a man of these things before he has tasted them. The life of the home is treated as more important than the size of the army.

Even the man who is simply afraid may go. This was practical, since fear spreads through an army. It was also merciful. No one is shamed, and no reason has to be given beyond the fear itself.

An army that sends its men home before the fight is saying something about what it trusts. The Old Testament shows these rules in use. Gideon, in the book of Judges, sends home everyone who is afraid, and most of his army leaves.

These are rules for ancient Israel's wars. They are not a manual for any army today.
passages.later:
Gideon's officers gave the fourth question as an order: ‘Whoever is fearful and trembling may turn back’ (Judges 7:3).

A psalm puts verse 1 into a line of worship: “Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7).

The New Testament changes the weapons altogether. “The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world” (2 Corinthians 10:4). It presents the cross as God's own victory: “And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross” (Colossians 2:15).
passages.asks: The law valued a man's first year in his house, his vineyard and his marriage above his use as a soldier. Ask what your work or your cause is costing the people at home, and whether you treat home as the thing the rest is for. And ask what you are counting when you feel outnumbered.

passages.t: Cities far away, and the cities of the land
passages.happening:
Two different rules follow, for two kinds of city.

The first is for cities ‘that are far away from you’ (verse 15). “When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace” (verse 10). If the city accepts and opens its gates, its people become forced laborers (verse 11). If it refuses and fights, Israel may besiege it. When it falls, the men are to be killed, and the women, children, livestock and goods may be taken as plunder (verses 12-14).

The second is for the cities of the land God is giving Israel. “However, in the cities of the nations that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, you must not leave alive anything that breathes” (verse 16). They are to be devoted to complete destruction, ‘so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
War in the ancient world was brutal. The inscriptions of Assyrian kings boast of cities burned and captives tortured. This law was written in that world and must be read in it. It must also be read honestly. Some of what it permits is terrible.

Begin with what it restrains. Israel's wars were to begin with an offer to end them. The Hebrew word in verse 10 is shalom, peace. A city could not be attacked until it had been offered terms. Moses did this himself with Sihon (2:26).

Now what it permits. A city that accepted became forced labor. In a city that fought, the men were killed, and the women and children were taken. The law treats women and children as plunder beside the livestock. That is in the text, and it cannot be explained away. These notes do not defend it. The law of the captive woman in the next chapter shows what could follow.

The second rule is harder still. For the cities of Canaan the ban of chapter 7 applies: nothing that breathes is to be left alive. The reason given is not race or land. It is worship, and the fear that Israel will learn ‘the detestable things they do for their gods’. This book has named the worst of those things, the burning of children (12:31).

The word behind ‘devote them to complete destruction’ is herem. A Moabite king of the ninth century BC used the same word on his monument for what he did to an Israelite town. The idea was known across the region.

The books that follow show the command applied at Jericho and Ai. They also show a Canaanite woman, Rahab, and her family spared, the people of Gibeon making peace and living, and many Canaanites still in the land long after.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua reports the command as carried out: ‘He devoted to destruction everything that breathed, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded’ (Joshua 10:40). It also records a treaty: “And Joshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live” (Joshua 9:15).

The prophet Isaiah saw where God is taking the nations: “They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks” (Isaiah 2:4).

Jesus said to a disciple who drew a sword to defend him, ‘Put your sword back in its place’ (Matthew 26:52).
passages.hard:
How can God command that nothing that breathes be left alive? And what of the rules for other cities?

This is one of the hardest passages in the Old Testament, and Jews and Christians have wrestled with it for centuries. A reader should feel its weight and not hurry past.

Christians who receive these books as God's word read the command about Canaan in several ways. Some read it as God's judgment on peoples whose guilt had built up over centuries (Genesis 15:16), and note that God later judged Israel by exile for the same sins. Some note that sweeping language of total destruction was usual in ancient reports of war, and that Joshua and Judges show Canaanites still living in the land. Some read these texts as a real but partial stage in God's making himself known, to be read in the light of Christ. The note on chapter 7, verses 1 to 5, sets out these readings and the cost of each. The site takes no side among them.

The Bible itself limits the command. It applies only to the named peoples of Canaan and not to Israel's other wars. It is never given as a pattern for later generations.

The rules for distant cities belong to the warfare of their age. They restrained it at some points, as in the offer of peace, and left much of its cruelty standing. They are not a model for any army, and nothing in them excuses forced labor, the killing of prisoners or the taking of women and children.

So it must be said plainly. No one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people. It names peoples of the ancient world. It says nothing about any nation, state or conflict today. Where Christians have used these texts that way, as in some preaching of crusade and of colonial conquest, the church has come to see it as a misuse.

The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: Do not read this passage quickly. Ask what in it troubles you, and bring that to God as Abraham did. Then notice the one fear the chapter names: that Israel will learn the ways of other gods. Ask what you are learning, without noticing, from the world you live in.

passages.happening:
The chapter ends with a rule about a long siege. “When you lay siege to a city for an extended time while fighting against it to capture it, you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit. You must not cut them down. Are the trees of the field human, that you should besiege them?” (verse 19).

Trees that do not bear fruit may be cut for siege works (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
In ancient war, to cut down an enemy's orchards was a way to ruin a region for years. An olive tree or a fig tree takes a long time to grow. Assyrian palace carvings show soldiers felling the trees around a besieged city.

Against that, this law stands out. Israel may use other wood for its siege works. It may not destroy the trees that feed people. The war will end, and whoever lives there afterward will need to eat.

The law is given as a question, which is unusual. ‘Are the trees of the field human, that you should besiege them?’ The tree is not the enemy. Even in war there are things that must not be treated as targets.

A chapter that began with horses and chariots ends with fruit trees. It does not make the earlier verses easier. But it shows that even here the law is pressing against the habits of its world, and that God cares about what is left standing when the fighting stops.
passages.later:
The first command given to human beings was to care for a garden: “Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15).

The prophet Micah pictures the peace God intends in terms of the trees this law protects: “And each man will sit under his own vine and under his own fig tree, with no one to frighten him” (Micah 4:4).
passages.asks: Even in war Israel was told to think about what would feed people afterward. Ask what you destroy when you are in a conflict, with a rival, a relative or a former friend, that will be needed when the conflict is over. And ask whether you treat as enemies things, or people, that are not.
